newsitem.title: USA: Enron reports second-quarter loss after big charge.
newsitem.headline: Enron reports second-quarter loss after big charge.

text.p: Enron Corp. Tuesday reported a $420 million loss for the second quarter as the oil and gas company took $524 million in charges for depressed profit margins and settling a lawsuit over a natural gas contract.
Enron also cut its 1997 earnings forecast, prompting PaineWebber Inc. and CS First Boston to lower their earnings estimates for the oil and gas company, based in Houston.
Enron stock slid $2.125 to $38.125 on the New York Stock Exchange and was one of the most active issues at midday.

Enron's second-quarter loss, equal to $1.71 a share, compared with profits of $117 million, or 46 cents a share, in the 1996 second quarter. Excluding the charges, Enron had operating income of $104 million in the second quarter.
Revenues rose to $3.2 billion from $3.0 billion.

The company said on June 2 it would take an after-tax charge of $450 million, or $1.81 a share, reflecting the full payment to a consortium to amend terms of a contract to buy gas from the British North Sea.

Enron had agreed in 1992 to pay a fixed price for the gas. But it withheld payments after market prices tumbled, and challenged the validity of the contract. In June, Enron lost the legal battle, but before the court ruling it agreed to settle the case with Phillips Petroleum, British Gas and Agip.

Enron, one of the nation's largest independent oil and gas companies, said it also took a one-time after-tax charge of $74 million, or 30 cents a share, to reflect depressed margins in the second quarter.
"The earnings effect of the settlement makes this a disappointing quarter," said Chairman Kenneth Lay.
The company said the removal of price hedges on its exploration and production activities has made it more dependent on oil and gas prices.

"Because prices for the remainder of the year are highly uncertain, we cannot forecast that we will be able to fully offset the previously booked hedge losses through price increases in the second half of 1997," it said.
Enron also cut its forecast for 1997 earnings by 30 cents a share to about $2.25 a share. The estimate excludes the one-time charges in the second quarter.
PaineWebber cut its rating on Enron's stock to neutral from attractive. First Boston, however, continued to recommend buying the stock, saying it is expected to reach $50 a share.
The company also said directors authorised the repurchase of 10 million shares during the second half of the year.

Separately, Enron said it holds the largest stake in the consortium that was the successful bidder in the privatisation of CEG, Rio de Janeiro's municipal gas distribution company, and Riogas, the gas distribution company in the interior of the state of Rio de Janeiro.
Enron said the winning bid for a 56.4 percent stake in CEG and a 75 percent stake in Riogas was about $576 million.
